title: China Outbuilds US Navy Two-to-One as Euronaval Data Flips the Shipbuilding Scoreboard
subhead: A Euronaval shipbuilding report shows China built 636,208 tons of combat vessels in 2024-25 against 270,509 for the United States — a role reversal from just two years earlier. The same week, an F-22 flew a live CCA as an airborne controller and Zelenskyy said Washington is holding up Patriots Kyiv already paid for.

sections.heading: Euronaval: China Built 2.3x US Naval Tonnage in 2024-25
sections.body:
The World Defense Shipbuilding report published by Euronaval, compiled by Flottes de Combat and the French maritime industry association Gican, puts Chinese combat-vessel construction at 636,208 tons in the two years to December 2025, against 270,509 tons for the United States — more than twice the US output, per Defense News.

The reversal is stark. In the 2022-23 edition of the same report, US yards produced 245,703 tons against China's 202,520 tons. China now accounts for more than a third of all naval tonnage built worldwide, and the value gap tracks the tonnage gap: $43.5 billion in Chinese combat-vessel construction versus $26.8 billion for the US.

Global naval construction overall surged to 1.47 million tons in 2024-25, up from 959,671 tons in the prior two-year period, with total value rising from $81.8 billion to $123.9 billion. Russia placed third with 149,056 tons, followed by India (76,430), Italy (53,700), then Turkey, France, Japan, South Korea and Romania.

The US Navy still fields the larger fleet by tonnage — 3.11 million tons of combat vessels over 200 tons as of January 1, 2026, versus 1.44 million for China — but that lead has shrunk from 3.22 against 1.30 million two years ago. Philippe Missoffe, Gican's general director, said the data shows 'a fairly substantial expansion of naval forces, and consequently of shipbuilding,' with particular growth in nuclear-powered attack submarines.
sections.whyItMatters: The US advantage is now entirely inventory, not throughput. Every year China outbuilds Washington this steeply, the existing fleet lead erodes faster than US yards can replace losses — which is the argument behind congressional pushes to allow allied shipyard work.

sections.heading: An F-22 Flew a Fury Drone as Its Wingman
sections.body:
The US Air Force announced that an F-22 Raptor carried out airborne tactical command and in-flight control of an Anduril YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft earlier this month, with the fighter pilot acting as an airborne 'quarterback' issuing high-level directives that the drone's onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed in real time — including maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.

Personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch ran the demonstration. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the service is 'driving urgency into every part of acquisition.'

This sits inside an aggressive CCA roadmap: 500 combat-ready semi-autonomous aircraft by 2032 and a total fleet of 1,000. Anduril's Fury already completed an end-to-end beyond-line-of-sight live-fire strike at Edwards AFB in July, and General Atomics' FQ-42A Vengeance was delivered to Creech AFB last month for test and evaluation.
sections.whyItMatters: The hard part of loyal wingman programs was never the drone — it was the command link that lets a legacy fighter task an autonomous aircraft without a ground crew in the loop. Flying it from an F-22, a jet with no two-seat variant and an aging avionics stack, is a harder integration test than flying it from a newer platform.

sections.heading: Zelenskyy: Washington Is Slowing Patriots Kyiv Already Paid For
sections.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told a US congressional delegation that American decisions on the war are 'hard to explain between friends,' citing delayed arms shipments and restrictions on intelligence sharing, per Defense News and Reuters.

Specifics: Ukraine is not receiving full explanations for limits on Starshield use needed to stage some drone strikes and defend against high-speed jet-powered drones; on three occasions in the past week Kyiv did not get advance warning of attacks normally provided by partners; and the Pentagon is delaying missiles already paid for through the PURL program, with one package awaiting Hegseth's signature. The Washington Post reported that Patriot interceptor missiles are among the held-up items as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian cities.

Zelenskyy also offered a trade: Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian oil refineries for 30 days — a demand Trump has made — if Washington supplies Patriot interceptors. He said he expects a Ukrainian delegation to meet US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Norway in the coming days.
sections.whyItMatters: The bottleneck has moved from production to political release. PURL was designed so allies could buy American weapons for Ukraine; if paid-for packages stall at the signature level, the program's value to European funders drops sharply — and Kyiv's refinery-strike leverage is being spent on interceptors rather than on territory.

sections.heading: Rheinmetall Buys Mangalia Shipyard for €138M
sections.body:
Rheinmetall and Swiss shipping company MSC won the auction for Romania's Mangalia shipyard south of Constanța at a purchase price of roughly €138 million, to be paid jointly. The site will be run as a dual-use facility with segregated security zones for civil and military work.

The immediate workload is Romanian government orders: two 96-metre offshore patrol vessels and two 43-metre diver support vessels for Rheinmetall Naval Systems. Tim Wagner, CEO of the Naval Systems division, said the company plans to 'expand and upgrade the shipyard comprehensively' and make it a hub for further military shipbuilding in south-eastern Europe. Rheinmetall has operated in Romania since 2024 through Rheinmetall Automecanica in Mediaș. The deal is expected to close within weeks.

The move follows Rheinmetall's €1.5 billion syndicated credit line — doubled early from €750 million — and the October 16 opening of a medium-calibre ammunition plant in Albacete, Spain, with capacity for around three million components a year.
sections.whyItMatters: European primes are buying yards, not just booking slots in them. Rheinmetall acquiring Black Sea shipbuilding capacity inside a NATO member gives it a sovereign European naval production base — and a foothold on the alliance's most exposed maritime flank.

sections.heading: Golden Dome Gets an Army Unit, but Its Money Is Still in Play
sections.body:
Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, commanding general of US Army Space and Missile Defense Command, confirmed at AUSA that an Army air defense unit has been 'earmarked' for Golden Dome for America support, though he declined to identify it. He described GDA as disaggregating today's packaged sensor-interceptor-C2 bundles so operators can use 'any sensor, best shooter, right C2' across the continental United States.

Col. Kevin Stonerook, deputy commander of Joint Task Force Gold — a 100-person NORTHCOM unit stood up in January — said the task force has run planning 'sprints' since February with roughly 300 stakeholders in Colorado Springs, and that the next sprint is set for end-October.

The schedule is ambitious and the funding is not settled. The Pentagon wants to field an early GDA version by the end of next year, with the full system by 2035. It requested $17.5 billion for Golden Dome in fiscal 2027 through a $350 billion reconciliation package, plus only about $400 million in base-budget R&D. Air and Space Forces Magazine reported in September that a dispute over the reconciliation bill could put most of that funding at risk, and lawmakers from both parties have complained about slow progress and inconsistent communication from the White House.
sections.whyItMatters: Assigning a unit and standing up a task force are cheap; paying for interceptors at scale is not. Golden Dome's end-of-next-year fielding goal now depends on a reconciliation bill that is not passed — and the services are already organizing around a program that may not be fully funded.

sections.heading: Two Smaller Signals: Navy Maintenance AI and Australia's Air Defense Gap
sections.body:
The US Navy raised Gecko Robotics' contract from an initial 5-year, $54 million deal covering 18 Pacific Fleet ships to a ceiling of up to $300 million — six months after the original agreement. Gecko's drones, wall-climbing robots and fixed sensors, plus its Komodo deck-coating scanner, are claimed to identify structural issues up to 50 times faster than manual inspection and to save up to $8 million in repair costs per ship. The Navy is chasing 80% fleet readiness by 2027; GAO data showed amphibious warfare ship readiness fell to 46% between 2011 and 2020 and reportedly to 41% in August 2025.

Australia, meanwhile, launched a formal tender for a medium-range ground-based air defense system for the Army. Canberra currently fields only a regiment's worth of NASAMS short-range systems for an entire continent. Options on the table include AMRAAM-ER extended-range missiles on the existing NASAMS architecture — Kongsberg Australia managing director John Fry said the company is 'definitely interested' — or a hybrid approach using Lockheed Martin Australia's June SM-2 firing from a trailer launcher with the Aegis combat system and a CEA radar.
sections.whyItMatters: Both point at the same gap: readiness and magazine depth, not platforms. A navy that cannot inspect hulls fast enough and an army with a short-range-only air defense umbrella are both underequipped for the threat environments their governments now describe.

sections.heading: Hegseth's Unannounced Israel Trip and the Gulf's Alliance Reckoning
sections.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Uvda Air Force Base in the Negev on an unannounced visit, three Israeli officials said. Netanyahu spokesman Doron Spielman confirmed the meeting and said the two discussed 'the threats in the region' and US-Israel cooperation 'both offensively and defensively.' Hegseth thanked Israel for hosting US forces numbering in the thousands. The Pentagon has not commented. The visit comes as tensions flare with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify, and a week before Israel's October 27 election — which Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of.

At the Global Security Forum in Doha, former MI6 chief Sir John Sawers said Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE are reconsidering their security relationships with Washington, arguing the US 'was the guarantor of their security' and that recent attacks on Gulf states were 'provoked by a U.S-instituted war of choice against Iran.' Qatar's deputy prime minister and defense minister, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, said attacks on a mediator were unprecedented, per Defense One. Sawers also rejected the framing that Europe is rearming because Trump demands it: 'The reason we're increasing money on defense now isn't because President Trump is telling us to do so. It's because the threat from Russia is much greater than it was before. And the reliability of the United States is less than it was before.'
sections.whyItMatters: The Gulf is the fastest-growing arms market on earth and its buyers are now explicitly hedging on US security guarantees. That repricing shows up in procurement — diversified suppliers, domestic production demands, and less appetite for US-only architectures — long before it shows up in any treaty.

bottomLine: Today's data point that matters is the Euronaval shipbuilding report: China built 2.3 times the US naval tonnage in 2024-25, reversing the 2022-23 position outright, while global naval construction surged to $123.9 billion. Washington is compensating with software and autonomy instead of steel — the F-22-controlled Fury flight is the most concrete demonstration yet that loyal wingman command links work from legacy fighters — but autonomy does not fix a shipbuilding base, and it does not deliver the Patriot interceptors Zelenskyy says Kyiv has already paid for. Europe's answer is consolidation: Rheinmetall is buying a Black Sea shipyard rather than waiting for one. Golden Dome, meanwhile, is assigning units and standing up task forces before its main funding vehicle has passed.
sources: Defense News (Euronaval World Defense Shipbuilding report; F-22/YFQ-44A CCA flight; Zelenskyy on US decisions; Hegseth-Netanyahu meeting; Golden Dome Army support; Gecko Robotics contract; Australia medium-range air defense), Reuters, Washington Post, Air and Space Forces Magazine, US Air Force, Rheinmetall, Defense One (Global Security Forum, Greenland basing), GAO, Gican/Flottes de Combat via Euronaval
